method: Pitch classes are read from note names with any number of sharps or flats, or from the integers 0 to 11, and duplicates are counted once; each name is reduced modulo 12 so C♯ and D♭ are the same class. Normal order takes each of the rotations of the ascending set, adds 12 to the wrapped notes, keeps the rotations with the smallest span, and among those keeps the one that is smallest when its intervals are compared from the top note downwards (Rahn). Prime form transposes the normal order to begin on 0, does the same for the inversion of the set, and keeps the lower of the two sequences, so C major and C minor both reduce to 0, 3, 7. The Forte number is a lookup of that prime form in the published table of all 223 set classes, with Z marking pairs that share an interval vector without being transpositions or inversions of each other. The interval vector counts, for interval classes 1 to 6, how many pairs of the set are that far apart, taking the shorter way round the octave. Symmetry lists every n for which transposing the set by n, or inverting it about n, leaves it unchanged. The complement is the set of pitch classes not in the input, reported with its own prime form and Forte number. The page was checked against the published prime form and interval vector of all 223 set classes, and a second implementation in Python agrees with it over a hundred inputs. Register, voicing and doubling are ignored, and nothing is claimed about consonance, tonality or suitability.
